recent_posts.title: Why You Need 3 Nodes // My Proxmox Ceph Cluster Project!
Boilerplates 0.2.0 release with new template syntax and repo structure
recent_posts.summary: Boilerplates 0.2.0 is a major update to a Python CLI tool for generating customizable Docker Compose stacks and infrastructure templates. Key changes include: splitting the CLI application from the template library into separate repositories, switching template metadata format from YAML to JSON for better ordering and Python performance, changing Jinja2 template delimiters from curly brackets to angle brackets to avoid conflicts with Ansible and other tools, adding a new 'secret' variable type with auto-generation support, adding remote upload capability for generated templates, and separating Docker Swarm templates from standard Docker Compose templates. A future 0.3.0 release with a new web interface and custom templating engine is teased for the next 2-3 months.

recent_posts.title: Caddy web server setup guide including Docker and DNS challenge limitations
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on walkthrough of the Caddy web server and reverse proxy, covering installation on Ubuntu via package manager, basic static site hosting with automatic HTTPS via Let's Encrypt, and reverse proxying Docker containers. The author highlights Caddy's simplicity for straightforward setups but identifies two pain points: DNS challenge support requires rebuilding the binary with xcaddy and a DNS provider plugin, and Docker-first workflows lack native label-based routing (unlike Traefik). A community project called caddy-docker-proxy partially addresses the Docker label issue but doesn't include DNS challenge support out of the box. The author concludes Caddy is excellent for simple non-Docker deployments but prefers Traefik for containerized environments.

recent_posts.title: Why using OpenClaw with flat rate AI subscriptions violates terms of service
recent_posts.summary: Using OpenClaw (an open-source AI agent tool) with flat-rate subscription plans from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI violates those providers' terms of service. Vendors like Google have issued bans for policy violations tied to third-party tools using subscription credentials for automated workloads. Anthropic initially locked users out, then pivoted to automatically billing extra usage instead. The core issue is economic: flat-rate plans assume human-paced usage, while AI agents run 24/7, and vendors also want users locked into their own ecosystems. The recommended safe alternatives are using API tokens (pay-per-use), local LLMs, or providers like MiniMax that explicitly allow third-party tool usage.

recent_posts.title: NetBird Setup Guide (New & Simplified)
recent_posts.summary: NetBird has been significantly simplified with a single-container architecture that replaces the old multi-service setup requiring external identity providers like Zitadel. The guide walks through self-hosting NetBird on a VPS, configuring DNS, running the installation script, and setting up routing peers via Docker. Key new features include a built-in reverse proxy (using Traefik) that lets you expose internal services to the public internet with automatic TLS, granular access control policies, optional SSO integration, and a visual control center for managing larger networks. The tutorial demonstrates connecting a MacBook via WireGuard mesh, accessing a Proxmox server through a routing peer, and publishing an internal web service publicly with optional pin/password protection.

recent_posts.title: How to migrate from NGINX to Angie web server
recent_posts.summary: NGINX has faced a turbulent few years: its original creator left F5, a core developer forked the project citing concerns about its open-source future, the Ingress NGINX controller suffered critical vulnerabilities, and as of March 2026 Ingress NGINX is officially end-of-life. Angie (ANG) is a drop-in replacement built by former NGINX developers that supports all existing NGINX configs with minimal path changes. Beyond compatibility, Angie adds built-in ACME/Let's Encrypt TLS certificate automation, native Prometheus metrics export with a Grafana dashboard, and Docker-label-based dynamic upstream discovery similar to Traefik. The migration process is straightforward: swap the container image and update the config directory path from /etc/nginx/conf.d to /etc/angie/http.d. For Kubernetes users, Angie also offers ANIC as a drop-in replacement for the end-of-life Ingress NGINX controller, though Traefik is recommended as a stronger alternative.

recent_posts.title: Getting started with OpenClaw (VPS Set-Up simply + secure) Tutorial
recent_posts.summary: A walkthrough of deploying OpenClaw, an open-source AI personal assistant, on a VPS using Hostinger's one-click template. Covers secure setup with Docker, HTTPS via Traefik, SSH key configuration, and firewall settings. Explains how to access the web UI and CLI inside the container, configure LLM providers (recommending flat-rate plans like Claude or ChatGPT Plus over pay-per-token due to high token consumption), set up communication channels like Telegram, WhatsApp, and Discord, and install built-in or community skills from ClawhHub. Includes a practical demo of using OpenClaw to monitor GitHub PRs via a cron job, along with security warnings about running it on production machines.

recent_posts.title: Uptime Kuma v2 is HERE // Breaking Changes & Safe Upgrade Checklist
recent_posts.summary: Uptime Kuma v2 introduces MariaDB support, Docker secret support, new image tags, and deprecates the 'latest' Docker tag. The upgrade requires backing up the data volume before migrating, as the internal database schema changes and migration can take several minutes for large datasets. For those wanting to switch from SQLite to MariaDB, the process involves exporting the SQLite database, converting it using the sqlite3-to-mysql tool, and importing into a MariaDB container. The 'latest' Docker tag is now deprecated and users must explicitly pin to v2. Alpine-based images are also dropped in v2.

recent_posts.title: Dokploy vs Coolify feature comparison for self-hosted deployments
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on comparison of two self-hosted app deployment platforms, Dokploy and Coolify, tested side by side in a home lab. Dokploy is favored for its Docker Swarm-first architecture enabling horizontal scaling, cleaner UI, broader Git provider support (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea), more build types (including Heroku buildpacks), and built-in cluster monitoring. Coolify edges ahead with native Cloudflare tunnel integration, support for multiple reverse proxies (Traefik or Caddy), more pre-configured database types, and built-in housekeeping features like Docker cleanup schedulers. The author ultimately recommends Dokploy for users who need scalable multi-node deployments, while Coolify suits homelabbers wanting simpler maintenance automation. Neither is recommended for integrating into existing infrastructure.

recent_posts.title: Minisforum MS-R1 ARM mini workstation review for home lab use
recent_posts.summary: The Minisforum MS-R1 is the world's first ARM mini workstation with UEFI boot support, powered by the Chinese CIX CP8180 SoC (12 cores, 28W TDP). It features 32/64GB LPDDR5 ECC RAM, dual M.2 NVMe slots, dual 10GbE ports, and a PCIe 4.0 x16 slot — all in a compact, well-built chassis priced around $500–600. Geekbench scores (1,326 single-core / 6,510 multi-core) place it between a Raspberry Pi 5 and Apple M1 Mac Mini. The main disappointment is idle power consumption at ~19W (improvable to ~14W via firmware update), which is significantly higher than comparable x86 mini PCs like AMD Ryzen-based systems that idle at ~7W. For general home lab use, x86 alternatives offer better performance, compatibility, and efficiency. However, for ARM-specific development and testing where something more powerful than a Raspberry Pi is needed without enterprise-grade costs, it fills a genuine gap in the market.
